newsitem.title: USA: Dow 30 notch 1996's 30th record closing high.
newsitem.headline: Dow 30 notch 1996's 30th record closing high.

text.p: The Dow industrials notched their 30th record for 1996 as quarterly earnings reports streamed in with hardly a nasty surprise and bonds were bolstered by fresh signs of a moderately growing economy.

"We're seeing for the most part a continuation of a favorable interpretation of earnings news coming out and today's economic reports support the thesis the economy is growing at a rate even Goldilocks cannot quibble with -- not too hold or too cold," said Jim Solloway of Argus Research.
The Dow surged 38 points to about 6059.
It was the Dow's third all-time high finish for the week and topped Wednesday's record 6020.81.
The S&P 500 rose three to about 707, also its third record close for the week and bested Wednesday's 704.41 record.
The NYSE Composite rose two to an unofficial record 376, topping the previous all-time high of 374.74 set October 7.

The tech-laden Nasdaq Composite slumped for a second consecutive day, off nine to about 1242, despite more good earnings news. The ailing computer maker Apple Computer late Wednesday reported a fiscal fourth-quarter share profit of $0.20 against expectations for a loss.

"Since the first week of September, the Nasdaq 100 is up almost 20 percent and we have over 30 percent gains in Intel and Oracle. ... It seems they want to take a pause," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter.
Apple rose 5/8 to 26-3/8, Intel lost 1-7/8 to 110-3/4 and Oracle was off 3/4 to 43-3/4. Microsoft fell 2-1/2 to 135-1/2.
Winners beat losers 14-9 on very heavy NYSE volume of about 479 million shares.
The long bond jumped 24/32 to yield 6.80 percent after a smattering of economic data. Weekly jobless claims rose to a higher-than-expected 340,000 for the week ended October 12.
September housing starts fell six percent, the biggest drop since January 1995. Starts fell to a 1.438 million annualized rate, weaker than the expected 1.47 million rate.
Industrial production rose 0.2 percent in September, slightly higher than expected. Capacity utilization was at 83.3 percent.
And lastly, the Philadelphia Federal Reserve Bank's business index for October fell to a weaker-than-expected 5.3 versus 13.9 in September.
Ironically, the stock market's gains come as the ninth anniversary of Black Monday looms.

On October 19, 1987, the Dow plummeted 508.00 points or 22.61 percent. But analysts noted one major difference was interest rates that were at 10 percent and rising in 1987 while they have steadied to under seven percent now.

As for fears about October corrections, said Solloway, a director of research, "I was scared in October 1987 and a bit concerned in October 1989 but these were Octobers where the market was out of sync with fundamentals. It's not like that now. It's just a little expensive. A five to six percent drop is possible over several weeks with bad news but it's not my idea of the end of the world after a 17 percent rise" in 1996.

Among individual stocks, PepsiCo rose 5/8 to 29-3/4 amid rumors that it could be a takeover target of Philip Morris, up 1-1/4 to 97-3/8. Company officials declined comment. Industry experts flatly dismissed such talk, saying the pricetag on any potential transaction would be an astounding $60-80 billion.

General Instrument lost 4-1/2 to 22-3/8 after reporting third-quarter earnings that fell short of expectations and warning that fourth-quarter and 1997 earnings will fall below consensus. UBS Securities downgraded the stock.
Among IPOs, Prentiss Properties, a REIT that has interests in 87 office and industrial properties, rose one to 21.
XLConnect Solutions, a unit of microcomputer company Intelligent Electronics, skyrocketed 12-7/8 points or 86 percent to 27-7/8 in its first day of trading.
Metro Networks, a provider of traffic reports, local news, sports and weather to TV and radio broadcasters, surged to 20-1/2 from its $16 a share pricing.
Micron rose one to 32-1/8 after Merrill Lynch said Micron is poised to report a substantial upside surprise when it reports earnings for the quarter ending in November.
Dow component Merck, which Wednesday reported unexpectedly strong quarterly results, surged three to 75.
Merck accounted for one-fourth of the Dow's gains. Schroder Wertheim upgraded the stock.
Informix lost two to 24-1/2 after reporting third-quarter results that fell short of expectations. CS First Boston and Hambrecht & Quist downgraded the stock.
Other stocks falling on earnings included Cirrus Logic, off 2-3/4 to 21-1/4, and TCSI Group, off 5-5/8 to 7-1/4.
The Nasdaq Composite fell 9.03 to 1241.96.
The S&P 500 index rose 2.58 to 706.99, a record.
(Figures official as of 1645 EDT/2045 GMT)
-- Wall Street desk 212 859 1721
